Mochi: Aligning Pre-training and Inference for Efficient Graph Foundation Models via Meta-Learning

João Mattos* Email: jrm28@rice.edu    Arlei Silva‡\ddagger*Computer Science Department; ‡Ken Kennedy InstituteRice UniversityHouston, TX, USA Email: arlei@rice.edu
Abstract

We propose Mochi11 1 Source code available at: https://github.com/joaopedromattos/mochi, a Graph Foundation Model that addresses task unification and training efficiency by adopting a meta-learning based training framework. Prior models pre-train with reconstruction-based objectives such as link prediction, and assume that the resulting representations can be aligned with downstream tasks through a separate unification step such as class prototypes. We demonstrate through synthetic and real-world experiments that this procedure, while simple and intuitive, has limitations that directly affect downstream task performance. To address these limitations, Mochi pre-trains on few-shot episodes that mirror the downstream evaluation protocol, aligning the training objective with inference rather than relying on a post-hoc unification step. We show that Mochi, along with its more powerful variant Mochi++, achieves competitive or superior performance compared to existing Graph Foundation Models across 25 real-world graph datasets spanning node classification, link prediction, and graph classification, while requiring 8∼\sim27 times less training time than the strongest baseline.

1 Introduction

Universal Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations that generalize across domains and tasks, regardless of the structural abstraction level (e.g. nodes, edges, subgraphs, motifs, or entire graphs). A central challenge in GFM design is task unification: how can a single model, trained once, support heterogeneous downstream tasks through a common inference interface?

A widely adopted solution is prototype-based classification[38, 20, 18, 10, 36]. Given node embeddings produced by a pretrained encoder, one constructs class prototypes by averaging the embeddings of labeled support nodes, and classifies query nodes/graphs by scoring their similarity to each prototype. Since these models are pre-trained using link prediction as a pre-training task, this elegantly reduces node classification, graph classification, and other tasks to pairwise scoring, by reusing the same mechanism across abstraction levels. Beyond unifying task formats, prototypes provide a parameter-free readout that accommodates arbitrary and previously unseen label sets at inference, which makes them attractive under few-shot budgets and non-trivial to replace: any alternative must preserve task unification across abstraction levels, support open label sets, and avoid introducing an inner-loop optimization step at test time.

Despite these advantages, previous works[1, 16] demonstrate pitfalls in adopting prototype-based methods for few-shot learning in other domains, such as images. In this paper, we build from the fact that prototype-based classification is a restricted special case of a constrained linear model, and that this restriction introduces three main limitations: (i) origin anchoring, where the decision boundary is locked to the origin (§2.1); (ii) convex-hull inclusion, where classes whose prototype falls within the convex hull of the other prototypes become provably unclassifiable (§2.2); and (iii) calibration failure, where the softmax probabilities over prototype scores bear no relation to true posteriors (§2.3). These failures are amplified by the pre-training objectives used in many current GFMs. Reconstruction-based objectives, such as link prediction [38, 20, 27] or topology reconstruction [36], favor embedding geometry aligned with pairwise connectivity rather than class discrimination [24], and post-hoc linear readouts on frozen embeddings are insufficient to bridge that mismatch.

To close this gap, we propose Mochi, a GFM trained via episodic meta-learning. At each step, the encoder receives a few-shot episode drawn from a node, edge, or graph-level task, a closed-form ridge head is fit on the support set, and gradients from the query loss flow through the solve to update the encoder. This aligns pre-training with the few-shot evaluation protocol, replaces the origin-anchored prototype readout with a bias-enabled linear head that addresses the limitations above, and yields a more scalable training procedure by not relying on negative-sampling-based objectives to learn transferable embeddings, reducing training time by 8∼\sim27×\times relative to the strongest baseline.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    Formal analysis of prototype limitations in GFMs. Building on prior work that casts prototype classifiers as a restricted linear family [25, 11], we identify three graph-specific failure modes, origin-anchored boundaries, convex-hull inclusion, and norm-coupled miscalibration, and show that link-prediction pre-training amplifies each (Section 2).

  • •

    Episodic meta-learning for Graph Foundation Models. We adapt the differentiable-readout paradigm [1, 16] to GFM pre-training, training an encoder end-to-end through a closed-form ridge head across node, edge, and graph-level episodes. Unlike prior graph meta-learners [46, 12, 5, 32], Mochi unifies all three task families at the readout interface (Section 3).

  • •

    Empirical validation. Controlled synthetic experiments isolate each failure mode; on 25 real-world datasets, Mochi and its variant Mochi++ match or exceed six GFM baselines at 8∼\sim27×\times less training time than the strongest baseline (Section 4).

2 Background in Graph Foundation Models and Pitfalls of Class Prototypes

(Universal) Graph Foundation Models.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be an undirected graph with n=|V|n=|V| nodes, adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}n×nA\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}, and optional node features X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}. A GFM can be decomposed into three stages [34, 35]: (i) feature and structural alignment, which maps heterogeneous inputs to a shared space, typically via SVD over node features or the graph Laplacian [38]; (ii) pre-training, in which a graph encoder fθf_{\theta} mapping (A,X)(A,X) to node embeddings {zv∈ℝdz}v∈V\{z_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\}_{v\in V} is trained to yield transferable representations; and (iii) task unification, which combines these embeddings into a single inference interface across node-, edge-, subgraph-, and graph-level tasks. Our work targets (ii) and (iii): we identify pitfalls induced by prototype-based task unification, and propose a meta-learning framework that yields a task-general, sample-efficient training procedure.

Prototype classifier notation and setup.

Given a support set ScS_{c} of labeled nodes for each class c∈{1,…,C}c\in\{1,\ldots,C\}, prototype-based classification constructs class prototypes pc=1|Sc|​∑v∈Sczvp_{c}=\frac{1}{|S_{c}|}\sum_{v\in S_{c}}z_{v} and classifies a query node uu via y^u=arg⁡maxc​⟨zu,pc⟩\hat{y}_{u}=\arg\max_{c}\,\langle z_{u},p_{c}\rangle. This reduces any task to pairwise scoring, providing a single interface regardless of the structural abstraction level.

2.1 Origin-Anchored Prototype Failure

The promise of task unification is that a single inference mechanism can be applied to unseen tasks without task-specific adaptation. Accordingly, the readout should be stable under geometric transformations that leave the task unchanged. Translation preserves the classification problem in every relevant sense: pairwise distances, affine separability, and inter-centroid distances are unchanged, so the task does not become harder. The proposition below shows that origin-anchored prototype inference is not translation-invariant, even though the task is.

Proposition 2.1 (Translation sensitivity of origin-anchored prototypes).

Let 𝒵={z1,…,zn}⊂ℝdz\mathcal{Z}=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} with labels y1,…,yn∈[C]y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\in[C], and let t∈ℝdzt\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}. Define translated embeddings zi′=zi+tz_{i}^{\prime}=z_{i}+t, and let pc′p_{c}^{\prime} denote the class prototypes computed from {zi′}i=1n\{z_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i=1}^{n}. Then translation preserves the underlying classification task, but under the origin-anchored prototype rule the pairwise decision boundary between classes ii and jj is unchanged after translation: {z′:⟨z′,pi′−pj′⟩=0}={z′:⟨z′,pi−pj⟩=0},\{z^{\prime}:\langle z^{\prime},\,p_{i}^{\prime}-p_{j}^{\prime}\rangle=0\}=\{z^{\prime}:\langle z^{\prime},\,p_{i}-p_{j}\rangle=0\}, since pi′−pj′=pi−pjp_{i}^{\prime}-p_{j}^{\prime}=p_{i}-p_{j}. In particular, the boundary remains fixed through the origin while the data cloud shifts by tt.

The proof follows directly from the linearity of translation and is deferred to Appendix B. Proposition 2.1 shows that translation preserves task geometry, including pairwise distances and class-centroid separations, while shifting the data relative to the origin-anchored prototype boundary. If the translation along pi−pjp_{i}-p_{j} exceeds the maximum within-class spread in that direction, all translated points fall on the same side of the hyperplane ⟨z,pi−pj⟩=0\langle z,\,p_{i}-p_{j}\rangle=0, and a balanced binary task collapses to 50%50\% accuracy despite remaining trivially separable (Figure 1a). The failure thus comes from anchoring the readout to an origin with no task-level meaning, not from poor embeddings. Prototype accuracy can therefore vary independently of representation quality. We verify this empirically in Section 4, and Appendix A shows that link-prediction embeddings naturally induce the triggering geometry.

2.2 Convex-Hull Prototype Failure

A second limitation of prototype-based inference is its reliance on a single centroid per class. This compression can be effective when each class is well represented by its mean, but it becomes brittle when the resulting class prototype is placed in a geometrically unfavorable location relative to the other classes. In particular, failure occurs whenever a class prototype lies inside the convex hull of the remaining prototypes (Figure 1b). In that case, the prototype of the class can never align with a query more strongly than all competing prototypes.

We formalize this failure under the origin-anchored prototype score sc​(z)=⟨z,pc⟩s_{c}(z)=\langle z,p_{c}\rangle, where pcp_{c} denotes the prototype of class cc, and we denote conv⁡(S)\mathrm{conv}(S) as the convex hull of a set S⊂ℝdzS\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}.

Proposition 2.2 (Convex-hull inclusion prevents unique argmax).

If pc∈conv⁡({pc′}c′≠c)p_{c}\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{p_{c^{\prime}}\}_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\bigr), then for every embedding z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}, ⟨z,pc⟩≤maxc′≠c⁡⟨z,pc′⟩.\langle z,p_{c}\rangle\leq\max_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle. Consequently, class cc can never be the unique argmax of the prototype scores.

The proof is deferred to Appendix C. Proposition 2.2 identifies a sharp geometric failure mode: once a class prototype lies inside the convex hull of the remaining prototypes, the prototype rule cannot assign that class as the unique winner. Thus, even if the underlying class remains recoverable, summarizing it by a single centroid can render it effectively invisible to the prototype readout.

Multimodality is one natural mechanism for this phenomenon, but it is not required. Any class geometry that places the centroid in an intermediate region can trigger the same effect, including cases where neighboring classes are simply too close or arranged so that one prototype falls between the others. The issue is therefore not multimodality per se, but the mismatch between a single-centroid readout and the true geometry of the class distributions.

Exact convex-hull inclusion is a boundary case, but it captures a broader instability. In Appendix E, we introduce a soft ε\varepsilon-inclusion variant showing that nearly included prototypes can achieve at most a vanishingly small score advantage. As a result, their predictions become highly unstable: small perturbations to the embeddings or support set can eliminate any residual preference for the class. An illustrative example is provided in Appendix F.

Structural Sources in Graphs.

Such unfavorable centroid geometry arises naturally in graph domains. In many link-prediction settings, node embeddings encode structural properties such as degree or local connectivity patterns, often through differences in embedding norm or direction [24]. As a result, a semantic class may contain structurally heterogeneous nodes (for example, both high-degree hubs and low-degree peripheral nodes) whose average embedding lies in an intermediate region that represents neither subgroup well. More broadly, when semantic labels are not aligned with a single compact region of the embedding space, the class centroid can be pulled toward competing classes and may even fall inside their convex hull. Thus, this failure is not restricted to pathological multimodal examples: it can arise whenever single-centroid compression is a poor match for the geometry induced by the encoder.

2.3 Calibration Failure

Beyond point predictions (Figure 1c), many downstream applications require calibrated probability estimates. Prototype classifiers typically form such estimates by applying a softmax to the dot-product scores: P⁡(y^=c∣z)=exp⁡(⟨z,pc⟩)∑c′=1Cexp⁡(⟨z,pc′⟩).P(\hat{y}=c\mid z)=\frac{\exp(\langle z,p_{c}\rangle)}{\sum_{c^{\prime}=1}^{C}\exp(\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle)}. These scores are convenient, but they are not naturally calibrated. Two structural properties make this especially problematic in the few-shot setting.

Prototype norms affect logits independently of class prevalence.

The logit for class cc is ⟨z,pc⟩=‖z‖​‖pc‖​cos⁡θ,\langle z,p_{c}\rangle=\|z\|\,\|p_{c}\|\cos\theta, and therefore depends on the prototype norm ‖pc‖\|p_{c}\|. This norm is determined by the geometry of the class embeddings (i.e. their location, concentration, and multimodality) rather than by class prior probability or any calibrated estimate of P⁡(y=c∣z)P(y=c\mid z). As a result, the softmax can systematically favor classes whose prototypes happen to have larger norms, independently of their true prevalence or predictive uncertainty.

Query norms control confidence.

The same decomposition shows that ‖z‖\|z\| rescales all logits and therefore controls the sharpness of the softmax distribution. Larger query norms produce more confident predictions, while points near the origin yield softer, nearly uniform outputs. In many link-prediction settings, embedding norms correlate with structural properties such as degree [24], so predictive confidence can become entangled with graph structure rather than reflecting task-specific uncertainty. Simple image-domain remedies such as L2-normalizing support embeddings [33] are therefore unsuitable here, since they erase the very norm variation that encodes this structural signal. Standard post-hoc calibration methods [9, 23] require held-out labeled data, which is unavailable in the few-shot regime targeted by prototype inference.

2.4 Implications for GFM Design

The failure modes above share a common theme: prototype inference is too rigid for task unification. It uses a fixed origin-anchored geometry, compresses each class to a single vector, and provides no mechanism for adapting the decision rule to the downstream task. This rigidity is particularly limiting for GFMs, where a single embedding space must support tasks with diverse label structures and decision boundaries.

These observations suggest a simple design principle for GFM inference: the readout should retain the few-shot appeal of prototype methods, while allowing lightweight task-specific adaptation at inference time. In Section 3, we instantiate this idea using meta-learning [14], formulating inference as a convex optimization problem over the support set that learns discriminative weights and biases without introducing a task-specific decoder.

3 Episodic Meta-Learning for Graph Foundation Models

Section 2 showed that prototype inference fails because it is too rigid: it fixes class weights to centroids, anchors decision boundaries at the origin, and converts dot products into confidence scores with no mechanism for task-specific adaptation. Replacing prototypes with a stronger linear readout at inference time helps, but only partially [16]. Ridge or logistic regression can learn weights and biases from the support set, yet they still operate on frozen embeddings produced by an objective that is mismatched to few-shot classification or just operates over the assumption that downstream tasks align with the pre-training objectives [41, 26] (e.g. link prediction, contrastive learning, etc).

We therefore shift the adaptation target from the readout alone to the entire training procedure. We propose Mochi, a Graph Foundation Model trained via episodic meta-learning [8, 1, 16] across node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks (Figure 2). In each episode, Mochi fits a closed-form ridge classifier on a small support set and updates the encoder through query loss. This preserves the minimal-data appeal of prototype-style inference while aligning training with the evaluation protocol. It also yields an efficient training pipeline: the episode head is solved in closed form, avoiding the iterative inner-loop optimization required by more expensive test-time adaptation schemes. As we show in Section 4, this alignment makes Mochi both competitive with strong GFM baselines and substantially more training-efficient.

3.1 Architecture

Mochi consists of a graph encoder fθf_{\theta} and a differentiable ridge readout. The encoder follows a common feature-alignment pattern in graph GFMs [38, 28, 43]: for each training graph we precompute a frozen initial representation X0∈ℝ|V|×dzX_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d_{z}} via SVD over node features and the symmetrically normalized adjacency (full construction in Appendix H.1), propagate it along ℓ=3\ell=3 hops of the adjacency, and concatenate the propagations into a per-node input stack [X0​Ak]k=0ℓ[X_{0}A^{k}]_{k=0}^{\ell}. A trainable GAMLP [44] applies node-adaptive hop attention over this stack to produce node embeddings zv=fθ​(A,X)v∈ℝdzz_{v}=f_{\theta}(A,X)_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}. Only GAMLP is meta-trained; the SVD and hop propagations are deterministic and do not receive gradients (Figure 2).

Given a support set with embeddings Zs∈ℝns×dzZ_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{s}\times d_{z}} (one row per episode example, constructed per task type as described in §3.2) and one-hot labels Ys∈{0,1}ns×CY_{s}\in\{0,1\}^{n_{s}\times C}, the readout solves the ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized least-squares problem in dual form:

[W∗b∗⁣⊤]=Z~s⊤​(Z~s​Z~s⊤+λ​I)−1​Ys,\begin{bmatrix}W^{*}\\ b^{*\top}\end{bmatrix}=\tilde{Z}_{s}^{\top}(\tilde{Z}_{s}\tilde{Z}_{s}^{\top}+\lambda I)^{-1}Y_{s}, (1)

where Z~s=[Zs∣𝟏]∈ℝns×(dz+1)\tilde{Z}_{s}=[Z_{s}\mid\mathbf{1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{s}\times(d_{z}+1)} augments the support embeddings with an all-ones bias column, W∗∈ℝdz×CW^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times C} is the weight matrix, and b∗∈ℝCb^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} is the bias vector. Query logits are then

Y^q=Z~q​[W∗b∗⁣⊤].\hat{Y}_{q}=\tilde{Z}_{q}\begin{bmatrix}W^{*}\\ b^{*\top}\end{bmatrix}. (2)

Why a ridge readout.

Ridge regression is the minimal linear readout addressing the origin-anchored failure of prototypes: the bias term decouples the decision boundary from the origin (§2.1). A post-hoc ridge on frozen embeddings cannot resolve convex-hull inclusion, which requires reshaping the embedding geometry. We therefore use ridge as the inner meta-training objective: its closed-form, differentiable solution (Eq. 1) lets query error backpropagate through the solve and update the encoder, making linear separability a property of the learned representation rather than one the readout must recover post-hoc. Logistic regression offers the same bias but requires an iterative inner loop.

3.2 Task-Unified Episodes

A central design principle of Mochi is that task unification happens at the readout interface. Every episode is converted into the same input format for the ridge head: a matrix of embeddings together with class labels. The only task-specific component is how those embeddings are constructed from the encoder output.

Node classification.

Each example is a node embedding zv∈ℝdzz_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} with label yv∈[C]y_{v}\in[C].

Link prediction.

Each example is an edge embedding zu⊙zv∈ℝdzz_{u}\odot z_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} (Hadamard product of endpoint embeddings), with a binary edge-vs-non-edge label encoded as a one-hot vector in {0,1}ns×2\{0,1\}^{n_{s}\times 2}. This puts LP on the same (Zs,Ys)(Z_{s},Y_{s}) interface as NC and GC; sampling details are deferred to Appendix H.1.

Graph classification.

Each example is an embedding z¯G=1|VG|​∑v∈VGzv\bar{z}_{G}=\frac{1}{|V_{G}|}\sum_{v\in V_{G}}z_{v} with a graph-level label.

The readout is otherwise identical across tasks: it receives support embeddings, fits Eq. (1), and predicts query labels. This gives Mochi a single training objective across node-, edge-, and graph-level problems, without requiring a task-specific decoder architecture.

3.3 Episodic Meta-Training

Rather than pre-training on self-supervised or contrastive-based approaches under the assumption of downstream task alignment transfer, Mochi is trained on the same few-shot prediction problem it will face at test time. Each training step proceeds as follows:

  1. 1.

    Sample an episode. Select a task type (node classification, link prediction, or graph classification) and a source graph. Construct a support set with KK labeled examples per class and a disjoint query set with QQ examples per class.

  2. 2.

    Encode the episode. Compute node embeddings with fθf_{\theta} and build task-specific example embeddings as described in Section 3.2.

  3. 3.

    Fit the readout. Solve the ridge problem (Eq. 1) on the support set.

  4. 4.

    Meta-update the encoder. Evaluate the ridge head on the query set, compute the cross-entropy loss, and backpropagate through the closed-form solve to update θ\theta.

The only training signal is the episodic query loss. As a result, the encoder is optimized directly for what matters at evaluation time: producing embeddings from which a small support set can induce an accurate linear decision rule. This training–evaluation alignment is the key difference from post-hoc readouts on frozen GFM embeddings.

Pre-training costs in Graph Foundation Models.

Link-prediction pre-training [38, 18, 13, 20] samples NnegN_{\text{neg}} negative edges per positive, for per-epoch cost 𝒪⁡(|E|⋅Nneg⋅dz)\mathcal{O}(|E|\cdot N_{\text{neg}}\cdot d_{z}); contrastive pre-training [42] scales similarly with in-batch negatives. Each Mochi step instead processes a single episode with ns=K⋅Cn_{s}=K\cdot C support examples and Q⋅CQ\cdot C query examples, fits the readout in closed form at 𝒪⁡(ns3+ns2​dz)\mathcal{O}(n_{s}^{3}+n_{s}^{2}d_{z}), and uses negative samples only for link-prediction episodes. Since ns≪|E|n_{s}\ll|E|, and node- and graph-classification episodes require no negatives, the per-step cost is dominated by a single encoder pass over 𝒪⁡((K+Q)​C)\mathcal{O}((K+Q)C) examples. Combined with the absence of an iterative MAML-style inner loop [8], this yields the 8∼\sim27×\times wall-clock speedup reported in Section 4.

4 Experiments

Our evaluation proceeds along two complementary axes. First, we use controlled synthetic experiments to verify the geometric failure modes identified in Section 2 under settings where the task structure is fully known (§4.1). Second, we evaluate Mochi on real-world node classification, link prediction, and graph classification benchmarks, comparing both predictive performance and training efficiency against existing GFM baselines (§4.2).

4.1 Controlled Validation of the Prototype Pitfalls

We present two controlled synthetic experiments that validate the first two pitfalls from Section 2: origin anchoring (§2.1) and convex-hull inclusion (§2.2). In each case, we compare the prototype classifier against a ridge readout with bias. The third pitfall, calibration failure (§2.3), is validated separately in Appendix G.3; full setup details and additional variants are in Appendix G.

Origin-anchored failure under translation.

We verify Proposition 2.1 on a balanced binary classification task in ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64}. We generate two Gaussian clusters with fixed separation and translate the embedding cloud by t​utu, where uu is the cluster-separation direction. Because translation preserves pairwise distances, the task does not become harder. Figure 3a shows that a bias-enabled ridge readout maintains near-perfect accuracy throughout, while prototype accuracy degrades toward chance as the origin-anchored boundary becomes increasingly misaligned with the translated data cloud.

Convex-hull prototype failure under multimodality.

We verify Proposition 2.2 on a three-class problem in ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64} where one class is bimodal and the other two are unimodal. As the two modes of the bimodal class separate, its centroid moves toward and eventually into the convex hull of the other class prototypes. As shown in Figure 3b, prototype recall for the multimodal class then collapses to zero, exactly as predicted by the convex-hull inclusion analysis, while the ridge readout continues to recover the class with high recall. This confirms that the failure arises from the single-centroid readout, not from the underlying task becoming unsolvable.

4.2 Real-world Datasets and Baseline Comparison

Experimental setup.

We evaluate Mochi and Mochi++ against six baselines across four families of cross-graph transfer methods: a vanilla GNN (GIN), a contrastive method (GraphCL), three GFMs (AnyGraph, GFT, GPF), and a prompt-based approach (GraphPrompt). All methods are evaluated in a kk-shot (k∈{4,8,16,64,512}k\in\{4,8,16,64,512\}) setting across 25 datasets spanning node classification (5 benchmarks), link prediction (10), and graph classification (5), with performance averaged over 3 random seeds. Dataset names, training pool, and per-dataset numbers are in Appendices H.1–I.

Convex-hull prototype analysis.

To test whether the convex-hull failure arises in real-world GFM embeddings, we compute the per-class AnyGraph prototype on Photo, Computers, and Cora, and measure each prototype’s distance to the convex hull of the remaining ones in the full embedding space (Appendix H.3). Prototypes with distance smaller than any hull-defining prototype are flagged as especially susceptible. Figure 4 visualizes the geometry via 2D PCA (distances computed before projection). Across all three datasets, multiple prototypes lie substantially inside the hull, confirming that the failure mode of §2.2 appears in real-world embeddings.

Post-hoc linear readouts partially recover AnyGraph’s frozen embeddings.

As a diagnostic, we fit a linear head on frozen AnyGraph embeddings and compare against AnyGraph’s shipped prototype readout and Mochi++ (Appendix H.2, Tab. 1). Post-hoc linear recovery narrows the gap relative to the prototype readout but does not reverse the main comparison: Mochi++ matches or exceeds this stronger AnyGraph variant on 3 of 5 NC datasets, while using a substantially lighter training and inference pipeline.

Training cost versus performance.

To evaluate the practical efficiency of each method, we plot training cost (wall-clock hours) against normalized aggregate performance across all tasks.

We compute a normalized aggregate score per method by averaging its normalized performance across all kk-shots for node classification, graph classification, and link prediction benchmarks. Figure 5 displays the resulting Pareto plot on a log-scaled cost axis. Mochi achieves competitive aggregate performance at a fraction of the training cost of all baselines (0.4 GPU-hours compared to 11–42 hours for alternatives, a ∼\sim27×\times speedup over the strongest baseline AnyGraph). The Mochi++ variant, which processes one episode per task type in each optimizer step, yields further performance gains at a modest cost increase (1.28 hours, still ∼\sim8.6×\times faster than AnyGraph) and remains an order of magnitude cheaper than the next-best method. This result underscores a central advantage of our meta-learning-based paradigm: our method avoids the expensive link-prediction pre-training based on negative samples by aligning the pre-training task with the inference procedure, enabling Mochi/Mochi++ to be more sample efficient.

Head-to-head comparison with AnyGraph.

Since AnyGraph is the strongest baseline, we provide a direct pairwise comparison (Figure 6). Mochi++ matches or exceeds AnyGraph on all three task-level aggregates. This reflects an architectural difference: AnyGraph jointly trains a large encoder across 15 LP source graphs, whereas Mochi precomputes frozen SVD and hop-propagation features once per graph and meta-trains a compact GAMLP encoder through the closed-form ridge head. Trained on a disjoint multi-task pool (4 NC, 18 LP, 5 GC source graphs; Appendix H.1), Mochi++ dominates AnyGraph on aggregate at substantially lower training cost.

5 Related Work

Graph Foundation Models.

Graph foundation models learn representations that transfer across domains, feature spaces, and task granularities [21, 35, 34] through heterogeneous pretraining signals: edge / relation prediction [27, 20, 38], graph-level contrastive learning, masked reconstruction, diffusion, structural vocabularies, and task trees [42, 4, 29, 36, 37]. Language-assisted methods align attributes and label spaces through textual descriptions [18, 10, 17, 3]; prompt and in-context methods adapt pretrained encoders through learned prompts, prompt graphs, or task-specific reductions [28, 13, 6, 2]; and a line develops task-specialized GFMs, notably cross-graph node classification via analytical attention over inductive classifiers [45]. Across these approaches, representation pretraining is typically separated from the few-shot decision rule used at evaluation time.

Task Unification and Prototype Readouts.

Task unification reduces node-, edge-, and graph-level prediction to a common inference interface [18, 13, 27, 20, 36, 37, 2], typically via a similarity rule or prototype classifier. Prototype readouts are attractive for their parameter efficiency, but impose a restricted geometry [25, 11]. This paper studies the consequences of that restriction for GFMs, where structural pretraining, multimodal classes, and norm shifts interact with prototype readouts.

Meta-Learning for Task-Adaptive Readouts.

Differentiable closed-form solvers and convex optimization layers provide task-specific classifiers while preserving end-to-end meta-learning [30, 31, 1, 16]. In the graph domain, several works apply meta-learning to GNN backbones for few-shot node classification [46, 12, 32, 19]; Graph Prototypical Networks [5] combine episodic meta-learning with prototype readouts, closest in spirit to Mochi; the differences are that Mochi replaces the prototype rule with a differentiable ridge readout and unifies across node, link, and graph-level episodes.

6 Conclusion

We revisited task unification in Graph Foundation Models from the perspective of the downstream inference mechanism. Prototype classifiers reduce heterogeneous tasks to a common pairwise scoring interface, but at a cost: we identified three structural failure modes, origin-anchored decision boundaries, convex-hull failure under unfavorable class geometry, and norm-dependent miscalibration, that are amplified by link-prediction pretraining. Post-hoc linear readouts partially correct these failures but cannot fix embeddings shaped by a mismatched training objective. Mochi resolves this mismatch by making adaptation part of pretraining: it trains the graph encoder through episodic node-, edge-, and graph-level tasks with a differentiable ridge readout in the loop, achieving competitive or superior performance to existing GFM baselines at a fraction of their training cost.

Appendix A Why Link-Prediction Embeddings Trigger Prototype Failure

The origin-anchored failure identified in Section 2.1 is not merely a theoretical possibility; the geometry of link-prediction embeddings makes it the expected outcome. Link-prediction training with an inner-product decoder A^u​v=σ⁡(zu⊤​zv)\hat{A}_{uv}=\sigma(z_{u}^{\top}z_{v}) produces embeddings with three well-documented geometric properties [24]:

  1. 1.

    Norms encode degree. For matrix-factorization-based models, ‖zv‖≈dv\|z_{v}\|\approx\sqrt{d_{v}}, where dvd_{v} is the degree of node vv. This arises because higher-degree nodes must produce larger inner products with more neighbors.

  2. 2.

    Neighbors align directionally. Connected nodes have similar angular positions in embedding space, since zu⊤​zv=‖zu‖|zv|cos⁡θu​vz_{u}^{\top}z_{v}=\|z_{u}\|\,\|z_{v}\|\cos\theta_{uv} must be large for edges (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E.

  3. 3.

    Embeddings cluster in a cone. For assortative graphs (where connected nodes share properties), properties (i) and (ii) together concentrate embeddings in a low-dimensional cone within a half-space. The embeddings rarely cross the origin.

Property (iii) means that embeddings typically lie in a half-space, so the origin-constrained prototype boundary is misaligned with any task whose natural boundary does not pass through the origin (Proposition 2.1).

Property (i) makes this particularly damaging for degree-correlated tasks. If class identity correlates with node degree (e.g., distinguishing hub nodes from peripheral nodes), the true decision boundary is a threshold on ‖z‖\|z\|, which corresponds to a sphere centered at the origin—or, in projection, a hyperplane at offset δ>0\delta>0. The prototype boundary at the origin cannot represent this threshold.

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 2.1

Proof.

We prove three facts: translation preserves the task, translates the prototypes uniformly, and leaves the origin-anchored prototype boundary unchanged.

First, translation preserves all pairwise differences:

zi′−zj′=(zi+t)−(zj+t)=zi−zj,z_{i}^{\prime}-z_{j}^{\prime}=(z_{i}+t)-(z_{j}+t)=z_{i}-z_{j},

and therefore also all pairwise distances:

‖zi′−zj′‖=‖zi−zj‖for all ​i,j.\|z_{i}^{\prime}-z_{j}^{\prime}\|=\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|\qquad\text{for all }i,j.

Hence the underlying classification task is unchanged. In particular, distance-based classifiers such as kk-NN behave identically on 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and 𝒵′\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}, and any linear classifier with an intercept can absorb the translation into its bias term.

Second, if

pc=1|ℐc|​∑i∈ℐczi,ℐc:={i:yi=c},p_{c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{c}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{c}}z_{i},\qquad\mathcal{I}_{c}:=\{i:y_{i}=c\},

then the translated prototype is

pc′=1|ℐc|​∑i∈ℐc(zi+t)=pc+t.p_{c}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{c}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{c}}(z_{i}+t)=p_{c}+t.

Thus all prototypes shift by the same vector, and in particular

pi′−pj′=(pi+t)−(pj+t)=pi−pj.p_{i}^{\prime}-p_{j}^{\prime}=(p_{i}+t)-(p_{j}+t)=p_{i}-p_{j}.

Finally, under the origin-anchored prototype rule, the decision boundary between classes ii and jj after translation is

{z′:⟨z′,pi′−pj′⟩=0}.\{z^{\prime}:\langle z^{\prime},\,p_{i}^{\prime}-p_{j}^{\prime}\rangle=0\}.

Since pi′−pj′=pi−pjp_{i}^{\prime}-p_{j}^{\prime}=p_{i}-p_{j}, this becomes

{z′:⟨z′,pi−pj⟩=0},\{z^{\prime}:\langle z^{\prime},\,p_{i}-p_{j}\rangle=0\},

which is exactly the same hyperplane as before. In particular, it still passes through the origin. Meanwhile, the empirical mean shifts as

z¯′=1n​∑i=1nzi′=z¯+t.\bar{z}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{\prime}=\bar{z}+t.

Therefore, translation leaves the task itself unchanged while moving the data cloud away from the origin, which can break origin-anchored prototype classification. ∎

Appendix C Proof of Proposition 2.2

Proof.

Since

pc∈conv⁡({pc′}c′≠c),p_{c}\in\mathrm{conv}\bigl(\{p_{c^{\prime}}\}_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\bigr),

there exist coefficients λc′≥0\lambda_{c^{\prime}}\geq 0 with ∑c′≠cλc′=1\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}=1 such that

pc=∑c′≠cλc′​pc′.p_{c}=\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}p_{c^{\prime}}.

Therefore, for any z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}},

⟨z,pc⟩=⟨z,∑c′≠cλc′​pc′⟩=∑c′≠cλc′​⟨z,pc′⟩.\langle z,p_{c}\rangle=\left\langle z,\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}p_{c^{\prime}}\right\rangle=\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle.

The right-hand side is a convex combination of the scores {⟨z,pc′⟩}c′≠c\{\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle\}_{c^{\prime}\neq c}, and is therefore bounded above by their maximum:

⟨z,pc⟩≤maxc′≠c⁡⟨z,pc′⟩.\langle z,p_{c}\rangle\leq\max_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle.

Hence class cc cannot be the unique argmax of the prototype scores. ∎

Appendix D Origin-Anchored Failure Example

Illustrative Example.

Consider four nodes with 1D embeddings forming two balanced classes:

Class 0: z1=−1,z2=0Class 1: z3=1,z4=2.\text{Class 0: }z_{1}=-1,\;z_{2}=0\qquad\text{Class 1: }z_{3}=1,\;z_{4}=2.

The prototypes are p0=−0.5p_{0}=-0.5 and p1=1.5p_{1}=1.5, and the prototype decision boundary ⟨z,p0−p1⟩=0\langle z,\;p_{0}-p_{1}\rangle=0 reduces to −2​z=0-2z=0, i.e., z=0z=0. This correctly separates the classes (all of class 0 has z≤0z\leq 0, all of class 1 has z≥1z\geq 1), giving 100% accuracy.

Now translate every embedding by t=5t=5:

Class 0: z1′=4,z2′=5Class 1: z3′=6,z4′=7.\text{Class 0: }z_{1}^{\prime}=4,\;z_{2}^{\prime}=5\qquad\text{Class 1: }z_{3}^{\prime}=6,\;z_{4}^{\prime}=7.

The task is identical: class 0 and class 1 have the same separation, the same margin, and the same balance. A kk-NN classifier or a linear probe with bias (boundary at z′=5.5z^{\prime}=5.5) still achieves perfect accuracy.

The prototypes become p0′=4.5p_{0}^{\prime}=4.5 and p1′=6.5p_{1}^{\prime}=6.5. The prototype gap is unchanged: |p1′−p0′|=|p1−p0|=2|p_{1}^{\prime}-p_{0}^{\prime}|=|p_{1}-p_{0}|=2. However, the prototype decision boundary is still z′=0z^{\prime}=0, which is now far from the data. Since all shifted embeddings satisfy z′≥4>0z^{\prime}\geq 4>0, the prototype score z′⋅p1′>z′⋅p0′z^{\prime}\cdot p_{1}^{\prime}>z^{\prime}\cdot p_{0}^{\prime} holds for every node (both prototypes are positive, and p1′>p0′p_{1}^{\prime}>p_{0}^{\prime}). The prototype classifier predicts class 1 for all nodes, yielding 50% accuracy on a trivially separable task.

This is the origin constraint of Proposition 2.1: the prototype gap is preserved, the task difficulty is preserved, but prototype accuracy collapses because its decision boundary cannot shift with the data.

Appendix E ε\varepsilon-inclusion

Exact inclusion (Proposition 2.2) is a boundary case. We introduce a soft variant that captures near-inclusion.

Definition E.1 (ε\varepsilon-Inclusion).

Class cc is ε\varepsilon-included if there exist λc′≥0\lambda_{c^{\prime}}\geq 0 with ∑c′≠cλc′=1\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}=1 such that ‖pc−∑c′≠cλc′​pc′‖<ε\|p_{c}-\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\lambda_{c^{\prime}}p_{c^{\prime}}\|<\varepsilon.

Proposition E.2.

If class cc is ε\varepsilon-included, then for all zz with ‖z‖≤R\|z\|\leq R: maxc′≠c⁡⟨z,pc′⟩−⟨z,pc⟩≥−ε​R\max_{c^{\prime}\neq c}\langle z,p_{c^{\prime}}\rangle-\langle z,p_{c}\rangle\geq-\varepsilon R. That is, class cc can win the argmax by at most margin ε​R\varepsilon R, which vanishes as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Appendix F Multimodal Convex-Hull Inclusion Example

Illustrative Example.

Consider a collaboration network with three classes of researchers: Generalists (A), who work across two subfields, and two specialist classes (B, C), each concentrated in one subfield. Suppose the GFM produces the following 2D embeddings:

Class A:a1=(−3,1),a2=(−3,−1),a3=(3,1),a4=(3,−1),Class B:b1=(−2,0),b2=(−1,0),Class C:c1=(1,0),c2=(2,0).\begin{array}[]{lll}\text{Class A:}&a_{1}=(-3,1),\;a_{2}=(-3,-1),&a_{3}=(3,1),\;a_{4}=(3,-1),\\ \text{Class B:}&b_{1}=(-2,0),\;b_{2}=(-1,0),&\\ \text{Class C:}&c_{1}=(1,0),\;c_{2}=(2,0).&\end{array}

The prototypes are pA=(0,0)p_{A}=(0,0), pB=(−1.5,0)p_{B}=(-1.5,0), and pC=(1.5,0)p_{C}=(1.5,0). Since pA=12​pB+12​pCp_{A}=\tfrac{1}{2}p_{B}+\tfrac{1}{2}p_{C}, class A is exactly included by Proposition 2.2. The prototype classifier never predicts class A, misclassifying all generalist researchers as specialists and achieving only 50% accuracy.

A linear probe, in contrast, can exploit the second coordinate to separate generalists (who have |y|=1|y|=1) from specialists (who have y=0y=0), achieving perfect classification.

Appendix G Additional Details on Synthetic Experiments

This appendix provides the full setup details and supplementary synthetic results omitted from Section 4 for space.

G.1 Origin-Anchored Failure Under Translation

Setup.

We verify Proposition 2.1 with a controlled binary classification experiment. We generate n=800n=800 embeddings in ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64} as two balanced Gaussian clusters separated by a fixed margin Δ\Delta. Let uu denote the unit vector along the cluster-separation axis. We then translate the entire embedding cloud by t​ut\,u for t∈[0,5]t\in[0,5].

This transformation preserves all pairwise distances, and therefore leaves the underlying task geometry unchanged. In particular, a distance-based classifier such as kk-NN would have identical accuracy for every value of tt. We compare the prototype classifier against a ridge readout with bias.

Results.

As shown in Figure 3a, the ridge readout maintains near-perfect accuracy throughout, absorbing the translation into its intercept. In contrast, prototype accuracy degrades monotonically toward 50%50\% as tt increases. This is exactly the behavior predicted by Proposition 2.1: the translated data cloud moves farther from the origin while the origin-anchored prototype boundary remains fixed. A handcrafted two-dimensional example is provided in Appendix D.

G.2 Multimodal Convex-Hull Inclusion Details

Setup.

We verify Proposition 2.2 on a three-class problem in ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64}. Classes B and C each consist of 100 samples drawn from a single Gaussian. Class A is bimodal, with two modes of 50 samples each placed symmetrically on opposite sides of the B–C axis.

We parameterize the mode separation by δ≥0\delta\geq 0. When δ=0\delta=0, all three classes are co-located. As δ\delta increases, the two modes of class A move apart, causing its centroid pAp_{A} to move toward, and eventually into, the convex hull of pBp_{B} and pCp_{C}.

For each value of δ\delta, we compute:

  1. 1.

    the distance from pAp_{A} to conv⁡(pB,pC)\mathrm{conv}(p_{B},p_{C}), corresponding to the ε\varepsilon in Definition E.1;

  2. 2.

    per-class recall of the prototype classifier;

  3. 3.

    per-class recall of a ridge readout with bias; and

  4. 4.

    overall accuracy of both methods.

We use a 50/50 support/query split and average all results over 20 random seeds.

Results.

As mode separation δ\delta increases, the centroid of class A converges toward the midpoint of pBp_{B} and pCp_{C}, eventually entering their convex hull. Figure 3b shows that prototype recall for class A then drops sharply, reaching exactly 0%0\% in the fully dominated regime, while classes B and C maintain high recall. Consequently, overall prototype accuracy plateaus near 66%66\%: effectively random on the dominated class and nearly perfect on the remaining two.

The ridge readout, in contrast, is not constrained to class centroids. Class A recall remains between roughly 8080–85%85\% across all values of δ\delta, showing that the task remains linearly recoverable even when the prototype classifier fails completely. The growing gap between ridge and prototype performance in the dominated regime confirms the practical relevance of Proposition 2.2.

G.3 Calibration Analysis

Goal.

This experiment complements Section 2.3 by illustrating two structural sources of calibration error in prototype softmax scores and comparing them against post-hoc alternatives.

Setup.

We evaluate calibration under two embedding geometries designed to isolate the mechanisms identified in Section 2.3:

  • •

    Origin-shifted. All embeddings are translated so that the global centroid lies far from the origin, simulating the half-space concentration discussed in Section 2.1. This stresses the norm-dependent sharpness effect.

  • •

    Varying-radius. Classes are placed at different distances from the origin, so that prototype norms differ substantially across classes. This stresses the prototype-norm bias discussed in Section 2.3.

For each geometry, we generate n=500n=500 samples across C=5C=5 classes in ℝ64\mathbb{R}^{64}. We report:

  1. 1.

    Expected Calibration Error (ECE) of prototype softmax probabilities;

  2. 2.

    ECE after temperature scaling, with the temperature fitted on the support set; and

  3. 3.

    ECE of ridge logistic regression probabilities.

Reliability diagrams are computed using 15 equally spaced confidence bins, and all results are averaged over 20 random seeds.

Results.

Under origin-shifted embeddings, prototype softmax is severely miscalibrated (ECE =0.44=0.44): large-norm queries receive overconfident predictions even when they are not far from the effective decision boundary. Temperature scaling reduces the error to approximately 0.220.22, but cannot fully correct it because the logits conflate directional information with norm-driven sharpness. Ridge logistic regression achieves ECE =0.065=0.065.

Under varying-radius embeddings, prototype miscalibration is smaller in magnitude but structurally similar: classes with larger-norm prototypes are over-preferred even when the query is far from their true decision region. Prototype ECE is 0.120.12, temperature scaling improves it to approximately 0.080.08, and ridge logistic regression achieves near-perfect calibration (ECE =0.005=0.005). The reliability diagrams in Figure 7 show that ridge logistic regression tracks empirical accuracy much more closely across all confidence bins.

Appendix H Additional Details on Real-World Datasets Experiments

H.1 Experiment Setup

Our set of baselines is diverse and consists of a vanilla GNN encoder (GIN), a contrastive pre-training method (GraphCL), three graph foundation models (AnyGraph, GFT, GPF), and a prompt-based approach (GraphPrompt) that is treated like a foundation model by fine-tuning a single prompt on all training datasets. All methods are assessed in a k-shot (k∈{4,8,16,64,512}k\in\{4,8,16,64,512\}) transfer setting across three task types: node classification (NC), link prediction (LP), and graph classification (GC). We consider 25 diverse evaluation datasets: 5 NC benchmarks (Cora, CS, Photo, Arxiv, Fitness), 10 LP benchmarks (Photo, Goodreads, Fitness, Gowalla, Arxiv, Cora, CS, Collab, web-Stanford, roadNet-PA), and 5 GC benchmarks (MUTAG, PROTEINS, NCI1, IMDB-Binary, COLLAB). For each task, we vary the number of labeled support examples from 4 to 512 (NC/GC) or use an 80/20 train/test split (LP) and report performance averaged over 3 random seeds. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB). Training costs differ substantially across methods: Mochi trains for 10,000 episodic steps in approximately 0.4 GPU-hours; Mochi++, which samples one episode per task type at each step, completes in 1.28 hours. To ensure fair comparison, all methods share the same downstream evaluation protocol: embeddings are frozen and fed to identical readout heads used during training (prototypes for all methods, except Mochi, which uses a ridge regression.).Evaluation datasets are held out from training for all methods. Mochi trains on a disjoint multi-task pool comprising 4 NC datasets (CiteSeer, PubMed, Physics, Computers), 18 LP datasets spanning academic and e-commerce domains, and 5 GC datasets (DD, ENZYMES, REDDIT-Multi-5K, ogbg-ppa), sampling episodes uniformly across tasks with weight ratio 1:1:1. All baselines are trained using the 15 LP datasets considered, optimizing for their respective training objectives. We implement the GIN baseline using the standard GIN architecture [39] in PyTorch Geometric [7], trained as a Graph Auto-Encoder [15]. GraphCL is implemented through PyGCL [47] library. We adopt the original implementation of all remaining baselines, found in their official source code repositories.

All methods share the same pre-processing: we compute node embeddings via a truncated SVD of the symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix (A~=D−1/2AD−1/2\tilde{A}=D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}, projected to d=512d{=}512 dimensions with 2 power iterations) concatenated with an SVD of node features when available. On top of the frozen SVD representation we precompute ℓ=3\ell{=}3 hop adjacency propagations and concatenate them as input to a trainable GAMLP [44] encoder. GAMLP applies a per-hop linear projection (512→512512\to 512), node-adaptive attention over the ℓ+1\ell{+}1 hops using hop-0 as the attention query, a weighted sum, and a residual 3-layer output MLP with ReLU and dropout. The resulting zv∈ℝ512z_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{512} is paired with a differentiable ridge readout head [1]. This readout solves the bias-augmented ridge problem in Eq. 1 in dual (Woodbury) form [22], enabling end-to-end gradient flow without inner-loop optimization steps. Episodes are constructed with variable support (k∈[8,32]k\in[8,32]) and query (q∈[16,64]q\in[16,64]) sizes per class, up to 64 classes, with ridge regularization λ=10\lambda{=}10 and label smoothing of 0.10.1. Training proceeds for 10,000 episodic steps using AdamW (lr =3×10−4=3{\times}10^{-4}, weight decay =10−4=10^{-4}) with cosine annealing and gradient clipping at norm 1.0. Mochi++ uses the same architecture but samples three episodes per step (one per task type), following [40]. For link prediction episodes, positive examples are true edges and negatives are sampled uniformly at random from a fixed pool of non-edges within the same graph, at a 1:1 ratio in both support and query sets; edge embeddings are formed via the Hadamard product of endpoint node embeddings. For graph classification, per-graph embeddings are obtained by mean-pooling node representations. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48GB). Mochi completes training in approximately 0.4 GPU-hours, Mochi++ in 1.28 hours, while baselines range from 11 hours (AnyGraph) to over 41 hours for GraphCL. For fair comparison, all methods are evaluated with identical frozen-embedding readout protocols: prototypes and logistic regression for NC/GC, and dot-product scoring for LP.

Few-shot evaluation protocol.

For NC and GC, we construct kk-shot episodes by sampling kk support examples per class; when a class has fewer than kk labeled examples (notably at k=512k=512 on datasets with small per-class label counts), support examples are drawn with replacement. A fixed number of query examples per class is used across all kk values, since query predictions are independent and the query count does not affect the trained model’s decision rule. For LP, we report Hits@1000 by sampling 1000 negative non-edges for each test positive edge, ranking the positive against the 1000 negatives, and reporting the fraction of test positives whose rank lands in the top 1000. On GC benchmarks based on TUDatasets (e.g., MUTAG with 188 graphs), reported numbers average across 3 random seeds, each using a fresh random train/test split.

H.2 Post-hoc Linear Recovery on Frozen AnyGraph Embeddings

Table 1 compares three scenarios on five representative node-classification datasets: AnyGraph with its shipped prototype readout, AnyGraph augmented with an additional linear head fit on top of its frozen embeddings (a diagnostic ablation rather than a benchmark baseline, since AnyGraph does not train or evaluate with such a readout in its original form), and Mochi++ with its ridge-based episodic readout. The main point is that replacing prototypes with a stronger linear head does improve AnyGraph, confirming that prototype inference leaves performance on the table. However, this gain is only partial: on Cora, CS, and Arxiv, Mochi++ still exceeds the post-hoc linear head fit on AnyGraph embeddings, while on Photo and Fitness the post-hoc head is competitive with or slightly better than Mochi++. Overall, the comparison in the paper is not altered: Mochi remains competitive with the actual AnyGraph system while using a substantially lighter training and inference pipeline. Following the main NC benchmark, each entry averages performance over all kk-shot settings.

H.3 Convex-Hull Distance Score for Real-World Prototype Geometry

To quantify the convex-hull prototype failure in real-world embeddings, we measure for each class prototype its distance to the convex hull of the remaining prototypes. Let {p1,…,pC}⊂ℝdz\{p_{1},\dots,p_{C}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} denote the class prototypes for a dataset. For each class cc, we compute

dCH​(c)=minw∈Δ⁡‖∑c′≠cwc′​pc′−pc‖2,d_{\mathrm{CH}}(c)=\min_{w\in\Delta}\left\|\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}w_{c^{\prime}}p_{c^{\prime}}-p_{c}\right\|_{2},

where Δ\Delta is the simplex over the remaining classes:

Δ={w:wc′≥0,∑c′≠cwc′=1}.\Delta=\left\{w:w_{c^{\prime}}\geq 0,\;\sum_{c^{\prime}\neq c}w_{c^{\prime}}=1\right\}.

Thus, dCH​(c)d_{\mathrm{CH}}(c) is the Euclidean distance from pcp_{c} to the convex hull of the other prototypes. Smaller values indicate that the prototype lies closer to, or inside, that hull.

For cross-dataset comparison only, we optionally normalize this quantity by the mean pairwise prototype distance,

d¯=2C⁡(C−1)​∑i<j‖pi−pj‖2,d~CH​(c)=dCH​(c)d¯.\bar{d}=\frac{2}{C(C-1)}\sum_{i<j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|_{2},\qquad\tilde{d}_{\mathrm{CH}}(c)=\frac{d_{\mathrm{CH}}(c)}{\bar{d}}.

This normalization is not essential to the geometry itself; it is used only to make distances more comparable across datasets of different scales.

For visualization, we project the prototypes to two dimensions using PCA and draw the outer hull in that projection. A prototype is highlighted in the figure when its convex-hull distance score is smaller than the smallest score among the prototypes that define that outer hull. In other words, we flag prototypes that are more interior, in the full embedding space, than any of the hull-defining prototypes. This criterion is used only for highlighting in the figure; all convex-hull distances themselves are computed in the original embedding space.

Applying this analysis to AnyGraph embeddings on Photo, Computers, and Cora, we find several prototypes with very small convex-hull distances, including prototypes that are more interior than the hull-defining classes. This provides direct evidence that the convex-hull prototype failure is present in real-world datasets.
